To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) urban growth in the MRB is not welfare-improving from the perspective of urban environmental amenities; and that (b) the current planning system, which is based on the idea of compact city, would lead to a welfare reduction in terms of environmental amenities.
the environmental costs of urban growth in the MRB are not sufficiently high to justify current urban planning policies, which tend to promote higher density levels.

(1) there is a positive and significant willingness to pay (WTP) for the preservation of undeveloped land, and (2) this WTP is not compensated by the environmental benefits associated to the reduction of density in urban areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the environmental benefits of urban compactness are large enough to offset its associated environmental costs.

the question of how much of the environmental benefits associated to urban environmental goods are lost when cities grow at high density levels, and whether this loss of welfare is compensated by a reduction in the environmental costs of urban sprawl.
the identification of the optimal urban growth path in the MRB.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MRB should grow more in terms of land area and less in terms of population density, and that this growth should be achieved by transforming rural areas into urban ones.
, in the MRB case, the optimal city is a city that grows in a more disperse way, but not at the cost of the surrounding landscape.

, at least in the MRB case, the environmental benefits associated with living in low-density cities would be greater than the costs of the loss of natural resources associated with the transformation of rural land into urban uses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the optimal city size in terms of the environmental amenities provided by the city to its residents is not a compact city but a dispersed city, where the urban environment is preserved by means of green belts and other environmental protection measures.
, when accounting for the environmental benefits of urban environmental goods, the current urban growth trends of the MRB are not welfare-improving.
, when environmental amenities are considered in the urban growth decision, the optimal city would have a more dispersed urban structure than that currently observed in the MRB.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the environmental effects of urban growth are not only a matter of the environmental consequences of energy consumption and pollution, but also a matter of the effects on the perceived amenities of urban dwellers, which are affected by both density levels and the loss of natural areas.
the environmental effects of urban growth are more complex than what is commonly assumed.
, when accounting for the environmental amenities provided by the urban form, the optimal urban growth is more disperse.
